::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .148", "p = .12", "p = .921", "p = .105", "p = .199"), Sentence = c("An omnibus Wald F -test (with Satterthwaite's degrees of freedom approximation) showed no significant effect of monster family on accuracy, F 2,238.37 = 1.93, p = .148.", "We obtained the same conclusion after analyzing the first 50 trials (F 2,237.96 = 2.18, p = .12).", "The test indicated no evidence that the effect of trial differed across families (F 2,134 = 0.083, p = .921), suggesting that the rate of learning was similar across all three stimulus families.", "This model produced the same pattern of the results: a significant effect of number of switches (b = -.049, t(110) = -3.13, p = .002), but no significant effect of block-size variance (p = .105) or interaction (p = .199).", "This model produced the same pattern of the results: a significant effect of number of switches (b = -.049, t(110) = -3.13, p = .002), but no significant effect of block-size variance (p = .105) or interaction (p = .199)." )), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. **What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 31 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. text.text: Self-directed learning is a major part of individual knowledge formation.

People often autonomously organize their own learning into "blocks": they practice a certain task for some continuous stretch of time, then switch to another task for another period of time, and so on.

Yet current models of intrinsic motivation highlighting epistemic factors such as novelty, competence, and learning progress make various predictions about the extent to which learners block, as opposed to interleaving, their practice.
In this study, we demonstrate that people tend to block in a multi-task setting where existing models of intrinsic motivation based on epistemic factors make ambiguous predictions.
We show that while epistemic factors can partially explain blocking, a simple repetition bias substantially improves our ability to predict choices.
Acquisition of versatile knowledge is not an easy feat.

Given the limited time, competing needs, and the complex dynamic environment, efficient epistemic development requires strategic decisions regarding which learning situations to engage in and for how long.

Several authors maintain that epistemic motivations, such as curiosity and interest, are cognitive adaptations addressing the challenges of knowledge optimization under limited resources (Dubey & Griffiths, 2020; Gottlieb et al., 2013; Ten et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Several authors maintain that epistemic motivations, such as curiosity and interest, are cognitive adaptations addressing the challenges of knowledge optimization under limited resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Dubey & Griffiths, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Gottlieb et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Ten et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: While mechanisms underlying the emergence of curiosity and interest are not fully understood, contemporary proposals unanimously implicate a metacognitive process of knowledge monitoring, which informs decisions about engagement in learning situations (Gottlieb & Oudeyer, 2018; Goupil & Proust, 2023; Murayama, 2022).
text.formatted: While mechanisms underlying the emergence of curiosity and interest are not fully understood, contemporary proposals unanimously implicate a metacognitive process of knowledge monitoring, which informs decisions about engagement in learning situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Gottlieb & Oudeyer, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Goupil & Proust, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Murayama, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, choices made during self-directed learning may also reflect simpler non-metacognitive strategies that are aligned with knowledge optimization but do not require complex computation.
The current study focuses on one such strategy that might underlie the so-called blocking behavior in self-directed learning.
In a multiple-task setting where mastery of each task requires several trials, the learner can block or group their practice by temporally bundling together several trials of the same task.
This strategy contrasts with interleaved practice, in which the learner deliberately alternates trials of different tasks.
For example, when preparing for a math test, the student could block by practicing exclusively quadratic factorization problems in one session and then practicing derivatives in another.
Alternatively, they could interleave by practicing problems from both topics in each session.

People seem to have a strong natural preference for blocking when given the freedom to direct their own learning, which is evident both from their choices (Kornell & Vaughn, 2018; Lu et al., 2021; Tauber et al., 2013) and persistent attitudes (McCabe, 2011; Rohrer et al., 2020).
text.formatted: People seem to have a strong natural preference for blocking when given the freedom to direct their own learning, which is evident both from their choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Kornell & Vaughn, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lu et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Tauber et al., 2013)</ref> and persistent attitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(McCabe, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Rohrer et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Normative computational theories of intrinsic motivation (such as curiosity) hold that humans are motivated to maximize their learning (Dubey & Griffiths, 2020).
text.formatted: Normative computational theories of intrinsic motivation (such as curiosity) hold that humans are motivated to maximize their learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Dubey & Griffiths, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In line with this perspective, formal models of intrinsic motivation involve epistemic factors like novelty (Gruaz et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2021), learning progress (Gottlieb & Oudeyer, 2018; Schmidhuber, 2010; Ten et al., 2025), and competence (Deterding et al., 2025; Lintunen et al., 2025; Ryan & Deci, 2000; Ryan & Moller, 2017), in explaining learners' decisions.
text.formatted: In line with this perspective, formal models of intrinsic motivation involve epistemic factors like novelty <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gruaz et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Xu et al., 2021)</ref>, learning progress <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Gottlieb & Oudeyer, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Schmidhuber, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Ten et al., 2025)</ref>, and competence <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Deterding et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Lintunen et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Ryan & Deci, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Ryan & Moller, 2017)</ref>, in explaining learners' decisions.

text.text: These accounts suggest that the choice of learning activity is driven by our motivation to master our environment, e.g., by diversifying the set of visited states (novelty-driven motivation) or by continually upgrading one's set of skills (progress-driven motivation).

It is unlikely that humans can perfectly optimize their knowledge, but it is plausible that we are equipped with heuristics that help us approach this computational goal (Dubey & Griffiths, 2020; Ten et al., 2025).
text.formatted: It is unlikely that humans can perfectly optimize their knowledge, but it is plausible that we are equipped with heuristics that help us approach this computational goal <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Dubey & Griffiths, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Ten et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In theory, computational models of intrinsic motivation can account for blocking behavior but their predictions about blocking vary.

For instance, in an environment with an unfamiliar set of tasks, novelty motivation would pull learners towards tasks different from those that have been recently selected (Gruaz et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2021).
text.formatted: For instance, in an environment with an unfamiliar set of tasks, novelty motivation would pull learners towards tasks different from those that have been recently selected <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gruaz et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Xu et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, learners driven by novelty are expected to switch activity often and exhibit interleaving, rather than blocking.

Progress-based accounts predict blocking especially when the set of tasks is hierarchically structured, such that high-level tasks can only be learned after the low-level tasks, or when the tasks are highly distinct in difficulty, in terms of underlying task complexity and thus learnability.
Tasks that afford higher rates of progress receive more attention (see Colas et al., 2019; Forestier et al., 2020; Oudeyer et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Tasks that afford higher rates of progress receive more attention (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Colas et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Forestier et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Oudeyer et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Variable task difficulties imply variable learning rates, and thus, variable learning progress across tasks.
When tasks are matched in terms of difficulty, however, progress-and competence-based models predict indifference, as matched difficulty implies comparable learning rates and competence across tasks.

Yet again, in a new environment with unfamiliar tasks, a competence-driven learner who engages with one task at a time may, for example, temporarily elevate their subjective competence of the chosen/practiced task and, as a result, repeat in the future (i.e., create a block).
In short, people often exhibit a strong natural tendency for blocking.
However, the mechanisms underlying blocking behavior are unclear.
Different theoretical models of self-directed learning can explain and sometimes predict blocking, but these models are also consistent with interleaving in certain contexts.

The current study seeks to document the degree to which existing curiosity models explain blocking behavior and contrast it with a non-metacognitive repetition bias factor, often overlooked by these models.
As a steppingstone to this main objective, we seek to establish and quantitatively describe the prevalence of blocking behavior in an environment with multiple learning tasks matched in difficulty.
Our task design was adapted from the study by Ten et al. (2021), where participants learn latent categorization rules in a free-choice task.
text.formatted: Our task design was adapted from the study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Ten et al. (2021)</ref>, where participants learn latent categorization rules in a free-choice task.

text.text: In that study, the environment consisted of four distinct stimulus sets (families of cartoon monsters).

On each trial, participants chose a monster family and attempted to guess -with subsequent feedback -whether a member of that family (randomly chosen for each trial) preferred to eat one of the two family-specific food items.
Each family had a unique (latent) categorization rule of a distinct level of complexity (and thus difficulty).
In our study, the environment consisted of three monster families that were matched in difficulty.
Our design implements the same categorization rule for all families.
Thus, the underlying task complexity is approximately the same for each family.

This complexity matching helps us avoid biasing individual choices and blocking behavior and ensures that variation in decisions stems not from systematic differences in task structures, but from the learner's own choice history, whether from historydependent epistemic factors, such as depleted novelty or plateauing progress, or from a bias to repeat the previous choice.
Participants (N = 121; 50.41% self-identified as female) were recruited on the Prolific web-platform.
Participants' age ranged between 19 and 68, with the median at 32 years.
Most participants were from the United Kingdom (65.29%) and South Africa (17.36%).
All participants reported being fluent in English (84.30% monolingual).
The monster stimuli were taken from Ten et al. (2021).
text.formatted: The monster stimuli were taken from <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Ten et al. (2021)</ref>.

text.text: Each family consisted of a number of members that varied independently along two family-specific feature dimensions.

For example, the orange squid-like monsters could have shorter or longer tentacles and more or less widely set eyes; blue bear-like monsters could be taller or shorter and have wider or narrower bodies; green "eye monsters" differed in eye diameter and neck length.
Food preferences in each family were determined by a hidden rule.
Abstractly, the rule was feature integration for each family (see Figure 1B).
text.formatted: Abstractly, the rule was feature integration for each family (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref>).

text.text: Each feature (e.g., height) was represented numerically and if the sum of the two features exceeded 7, food A was preferred, and if the sum was less than 7, food B was preferred.
We excluded monsters whose sum of feature was equal to 7 for simplicity.
Thus, out of the 36 monsters available from each family, we used 30 whose sum of feature values was not equal to 7.
Since the underlying rule complexity was virtually the same in each family, the learning rates were expected to be similar across the families.

What does this monster like to eat?
Each trial started with a self-paced choice screen, on which the participant was prompted to choose a family to interact with.

After making a choice, the participant was presented with a randomly drawn individual from the chosen family (see B) and was prompted to indicate what they thought this individual preferred to eat (as well as how confident they were in their guess).
The guess and the confidence level were measured using a single slider widget.
Moving the slider closer to one of the answer options indicated more confidence in that option.
Placing the slider thumb in the middle of the slider deactivated the submit button underneath, while placing it anywhere else activated it.
Thus, participants were forced to guess one of the options but could indicate their level of confidence.
As a visual aid, a confidence scale appeared underneath the option that the participant was committing to.
This scale reflected the confidence level (from one's subjective minimum to their subjective maximum) that corresponded to the position of the slider thumb.
Upon clicking the submit button, participants were given visual and auditory feedback signifying if the monster had accepted the food (saying "Yum") or rejected it (saying "Yuck").
B. Each family consisted of 30 unique individuals.
The example above shows all members of the "blue bears" family.
The individuals varied along 2 dimensions (e.g., height and width).
The classification rule was based on the combination of the two dimensions.
Individuals whose sum of values on both dimensions exceeded 7 preferred one type of food.
Individuals whose sum of values on both dimensions was less than 7 preferred the other type of food.
We excluded monsters whose sum of features was equal to 7 to keep the symmetry of the rule and keep food preferences in each family balanced.
Repetition bias in self-directed learning
Our task procedure was also based on Ten et al. (2021).
text.formatted: Our task procedure was also based on <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Ten et al. (2021)</ref>.

text.text: We modified the experiment to match the objective difficulty of the learning activities.
In the main part, we asked participants to try to master three distinct but similarly difficult options.
After providing informed consent, participants read the task instructions (see S1.).
Participants completed a series of 180 self-selected, self-paced trials.
For each trial, a participant chose an activity, attempted it, and then received accuracy feedback (Figure 1).
text.formatted: For each trial, a participant chose an activity, attempted it, and then received accuracy feedback (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Each activity consisted of a family of fictional monster characters, each with a preference for one of two family-specific food items.

For example, in one activity, a family of pink bunny-like monsters liked either bacon or apples, while in another family of orange squid-like monsters, individuals preferred either grapes or avocados.
Participants started the main task at the choice screen, where they saw 3 clickable icons representing each monster family.
Upon choosing a family, participants saw a randomly selected member of that family and were prompted to guess its preference of food.
Participant's guesses were graded, rather than categorical.
Participants moved a slider towards a food option they wanted to guess.
The initial position of the slider was neutral (center), and the proximity to a food item indicated their subjective confidence.
After responding with a confidence-graded guess, participants received immediate feedback on whether their guess was accurate.
Next, they were taken to the choice screen again to commence the next trial.
A trial counter was always visible on the screen.
Both family choices and food-preference guesses were self-paced.
Once a family was chosen, an individual monster was randomly sampled without replacement.
If all members of a family were sampled, the sampling was re-randomized and reset.
This ensured that participants could see all members of a given family at least once, if they played that family enough.
There were 180 free-choice trials in total; this means that if each family was chosen an equal number of times, the participant would see each monster twice.
Thus, with ideal inference and memory, all 3 families could be mastered over the course of the task.

After completing the main part of the task, participants took two tests which followed the same format as the main task, except that monster families were chosen at random and no feedback was provided.
Participants were informed about testing at the beginning of the main part of the task.
The tests consisted of 90 interleaved trials, presenting each of the 30 individuals from each monster family in random order.

Due to a programming error, 10 to 18 of 90 test items in test 1 were invalid and thus we excluded them from the analyses (each participant was tested on 10 to 18 monster individuals whose sum of feature values was exactly 7, which was undefined for the categorization rule; see Section 3.2).
Test 1 was administered immediately after the free-choice learning phase, and test 2 was administered 2 days later.
All 121 participants completed test 1, but only 114 completed test 2 (5.79% dropout).
We used a conditional logit model (Lewis-Beck et al., 2004) to estimate the effects of various factors of learning activities (explained below) on individual participants' trial-by-trial choices.

Each model in our comparison set included a combination of existing theoretical factors: novelty (NOV), objective competence as percent correct (PC), and learning progress (LP).
Beyond existing theoretical models, we also included a measure of recent subjective confidence (CONF), based on self-reported measures of decision confidence.
Critically, some models included the repetition-bias component (REP) to examine if this bias explains the behavior above and beyond other theoretical factors.
All factors were derived from the observed choices and guesses.

To ensure that participants' choices reflected an appropriate level of task engagement, rather than clicking through the task because it is too easy or too difficult, we analyzed changes in accuracy over time.
The task should be sufficiently engaging if the participants do not get stuck at floor performance (around 50%) or quickly reach ceiling performance (around 100%).

To assess learning, we fitted a generalized mixed model of trial-by-trial binary response accuracy as a function of family-specific number of trials (correct ∼ trialsPerFam + (trialsPerFam | id), binary mixed-effects logistic regression with the logit link function).

We were primarily interested in the fixed effect of the trialsPerFam variable which would indicate the extent to which the probability of responding correctly increased with more experience with a monster family.

The effect was positive and significant (b = 0.26, z = 10.61, p < .001; see Figure 2A-B), suggesting that on average, participants improved their performance as they gained more experience in each family.

text.text: Thus, participants seem to have engaged in the task enough to learn the hidden rules of the task.
To rule out the possibility that participants may have learned too quickly and became less engaged throughout the task, we looked at their accuracy on the immediate test.
Specifically, we counted the proportion of correct responses in each participant and each family.
There were only three instances (out of 121 × 3) where a participant responded correctly to all test stimuli in a family.
None of the participants aced all three families and the majority of participants scored between 60% and 90% (Figure 2C).

text.text: Thus, while our participants improved convincingly in our task, they have not reached ceiling performance during learning.

While we intended to minimize the variation in difficulty across families by using the same categorization rule everywhere, the unique visual elements within a family could have interacted with the conspicuousness of the rule.

E.g., the "blue bears" family varied in terms of height and width (see Figure 1), so it could have been more natural to integrate the two features into a single "size" feature, compared to the "squid" family varying in tentacle length and eye-gap size.
text.formatted: E.g., the "blue bears" family varied in terms of height and width (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>), so it could have been more natural to integrate the two features into a single "size" feature, compared to the "squid" family varying in tentacle length and eye-gap size.

text.text: Thus, it was important to verify that monster families did not systematically differ in difficulty.
We used a linear mixed-effects model of accuracy (proportion of correct responses) in the first 30 trials with (dummy coded) monster family as a fixed effect and random intercepts by participant.
An omnibus Wald F -test (with Satterthwaite's degrees of freedom approximation) showed no significant effect of monster family on accuracy, F 2,238.37 = 1.93, p = .148.
Thus, the observed differences in accuracy in the first 30 trials due to family were no greater than what would be expected by chance.
We obtained the same conclusion after analyzing the first 50 trials (F 2,237.96 = 2.18, p = .12).
Our sample showed no quantitative evidence that monster families differed in difficulty.
As a supplementary analysis, we tested whether the rate of learning differed across stimulus families.
This analysis was performed on a dataset where individual trials (within each family) were grouped into incremental bins of 10 (trials 1-10, 11-20, 21-30, etc.).

We removed all groups for which there were fewer than 100 observations to conservatively avoid unreliable estimates for bins with fewer trials (note that this criterion filtered out bins with higher trial counts: all participants played at least 10 trials of each family, but fewer participants played 100 trials of a single family).
This gave us 141 accuracy data points, each corresponding to an aggregate of over 100 responses.

We conducted an incremental F -test comparing (1) a baseline model which included family-wise trial and the categorical family index as main effects, and (2) a full model which additionally included their interaction.
The test indicated no evidence that the effect of trial differed across families (F 2,134 = 0.083, p = .921), suggesting that the rate of learning was similar across all three stimulus families.

These results support the assumption that the potential effects of metacognitive factors can be attributed exclusively to choice and learning history, rather than some systematic variation in the structure of the tasks.

text.text: While there is a lot of diversity in how people organize their learning, the tendency to block is apparent: most people show uninterrupted series of trials on the same task.
We examine two aspects of blocking behavior: total number of switches and blocksize variance.
For each trial, switching was defined as a binary variable, such that switch = 1 if a participant chose a task different from the previous trial's task.
Blocks were defined as trials between consecutive switches.

While the variance of the block size is not a theoretically meaningful quantity, it allowed us to quantify the regularity of blocking behavior and distinguish between cases like aaabbbccc and aaaabbcc which have the same number of switches, but the former is more regularly blocked than the latter.
Thus, block-size variance captures an aspect of blocking distinct from the frequency of switching.
We use log-transformed values of block-size variance in further analyses, as the raw distribution had a long tail.
We compared the distributions of both quantities against what would be expected from a model that chooses randomly on every trial.
The expected number of switches and the log of block-size variance from this Random model can be derived exactly from the definitions of categorical and geometric random variables (see S4.).
The expected number of switches in 180 trials is ≈ 119.3 and the (log) of block-size variance is ≈ -0.2877, which are shown as green lines in Figure 3C-D.

text.text: The plots show that these values fall outside how 80% of participants behaved.
Therefore, over 80% of participants switched less frequently and had more variable block sizes than expected by chance.
These results also indicate that most people did not show extreme blocking or interleaving, which would result in low block-size variance (see bottom 20% in Figure 3B-D).

text.text: Switching less had a positive effect on learning.
Participants who switched less (i.e., blocked more) tended to perform significantly better on the subsequent immediate test.

This was revealed by a linear model of the immediate test accuracy (mean correct) as a function of (centered) number of switches and block-size variance (accuracy ∼ nSwitches * blockSizeVar) where the effect of number of switches was significant (b = -.045, t(117) = -2.94, p = .004).
The effect of switching frequency on delayed test accuracy was also significant (b = -.050, t(110) = -3.37, p = .001).
Thus, blocking (viz. less switching) was associated with better learning.
Note that the exclusion of invalid test items on test 1 (see 2.3) inflates the standard errors, but keeps the estimates unbiased.

Inflated standard errors do not threaten the validity of significant effects of number of switches, but could potentially hide the effects of the blockSizeVar predictor and its interaction with the number of switches.
To address this potential issue, we fitted a linear model of the delayed test accuracy again, this time keeping only the valid items that were present on test 1.

This model produced the same pattern of the results: a significant effect of number of switches (b = -.049, t(110) = -3.13, p = .002), but no significant effect of block-size variance (p = .105) or interaction (p = .199).
While not entirely definitive, this result suggests that the removal of ambiguous items on test 1 was unlikely to drastically change any of the observed effects.

In this study, we explored the human tendency to organize their learning into coherent blocks of trials of the same task.

As in other similar settings where learners were free to choose what to learn (Flesch et al., 2018; Tauber et al., 2013), participants in our study tended to block rather than interleave trials of multiple activities.

text.text: Notably, we observe blocking behavior in an environment with difficulty-matched tasks, where existing formal models of intrinsic motivation provide ambiguous predictions.
Accounting for repetition bias significantly improved the predictive accuracy of the existing theoretical decision/motivation models.
Nevertheless, the theoretical predictors (NOV, PC, and CONF) improved the performance of choice-models that included the repetition bias component.
Overall, our results underscore the role of repetition bias in self-directed learning, perhaps much more than researchers typically expect.
We observed a large effect size of repetition bias on predictive accuracy and a characteristic negative effect of block time on switching.
Moreover, we found evidence that repetition bias itself is partially modulated by epistemic factors studied in curiosity literature.
However, our study is limited in definitively answering whether repetition bias is a genuine cause of blocking or whether it reflects influences of unforeseen factors.
One potential interpretation of the importance of repetition is that learners seek to avoid effort and therefore engage in blocked practice as a heuristic.
Due to its computational simplicity, the literature has associated repetition bias with minimizing effort as opposed to reducing switching costs.
For example, Mittelstädt et al. (2018) showed that while repetition bias can be reduced by minimizing task-switching costs, it cannot be reversed by making switching advantageous.

text.text: Here, policy perseveration (along with repetition bias) is explained as a resource-rational solution for balancing rewards and computational complexity.
At the same time, we could also interpret blocking as strategic toward optimal learning.

Many empirical findings in the science of learning (Privitera et al., 2023, see) suggest that blocking, compared to interleaving, is often suboptimal for learning (Kornell & Vaughn, 2018; Yan et al., 2020).

text.text: However, our findings about the positive effects of blocking on learning (see 3.2) suggest that blocking might be compatible and perhaps complementary to efficient learning strategies predicted by theories of intrinsically motivated self-directed learning (also see Flesch et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2021, for additional reports of positive effects of blocking on learning).

text.text: Complex learning tasks like the one used in this experiment require some degree of familiarization to enable learners to construct coherent task representations, including self-efficacy beliefs.
Without such representations, learners may not be able to effectively execute optimal strategies like progress maximization.
Thus, blocking due to repetition bias might still act as a scaffold for learners to build up robust task representations enabling more effective resource allocation for learning in the future.
Blocking could also reflect an optimal learning strategy if participants are aware of the shared structure between the tasks in the environment.
In our study, all families had the same underlying categorization rule -feature summation.
If mastering the rule in one family allowed one to become better in others, it would make sense for the learner to allocate an uninterrupted chunk of time to learning a single family.
Our models did not account for these considerations.

However, we consider generalization unlikely to have been prominent in our study, because participants were deliberately not informed about the common rule in the environment and because of how nontrivial it would be to transfer the knowledge from one family to another.

To expand on the latter point, the summation rule acquired in one family cannot be directly applied in another, because different families have their own unique set of visual features and classes (types of food).
Nevertheless, we could not fully rule out this account because it was difficult to disentangle rule generalization from the general learning ability.
A simple way to strengthen our conclusions would be to introduce additional variable features as distractors and/or to explicitly instruct participants that the stimulus families are unrelated.

It is important to keep in mind that although our analyses render epistemic predictors as significant but relatively weak determinants of blocking, the genuine relationship between metacognition and repeating choices may be stronger.
Like all models, the curiosity models used in our study are rather crude approximations of theoretical constructs.
This also concerns our subjective confidence measure, as aggregate selfreported confidence is likely different from true subjective estimate of task confidence.

Both novelty and learning progress have been variously defined in the past (see Barto et al., 2013; Oudeyer & Kaplan, 2007), and there might be other conceptualizations or formulations that would be consistent with blocking without a repetition bias.

text.text: Combining the characteristics of the environment used in the current study with those used to study latent learning progress might help determine if such models can account for something a simple repetition bias cannot.
It appears though that repetition bias is the simplest strategy imaginable that enables the initial learning scaffolding to take place.
A subtle but important limitation of our design is the very decision to equate the complexity of the categorization rule across stimulus families.

Existing curiosity models (e.g., Poli et al., 2024; Ten et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021) seem to focus on different aspects of self-directed learning: what makes the learner select a task from a set of alternatives, and what sustains the learner's attention on the selected task.

text.text: Minimizing discrepancies in task difficulties may have reduced our ability to assess the selection aspect of the process.
This means that the conditional logit models used in our study may be limited not only by specification gaps, but also by insufficient variability in task selection features.
These concerns, however, are less applicable to the survival model that quantifies the role of epistemic factors on repetition.

Thus, while our design might be limited in gauging how strongly repetition bias and epistemic factors each pull on initial task engagement (selection), it should be appropriate for examining the relationship between repetition and epistemic factors (sustenance), which is what the last analysis in Section 3.4 addressed.
Different fields focus on different factors underlying self-directed learning.
Curiosity researchers highlight epistemic factors, such as novelty, subjective competence and learning progress.
Researchers in the science of learning emphasize the role of task spacing and sequencing, including blocking vs. interleaving behaviors.
Researchers in the task-switching literature care mostly about switching costs.
All of these fields are interested in self-directed decision-making in learning contexts but are not well integrated.
Our study represents a step towards demonstrating the potential of examining blocking behavior (and more generally, self-directed learning) from a multi-disciplinary perspective.

To decide on how to define global task confidence for modeling, we computed a running mean of confidence judgments for different window sizes between 1 and 15.
For each window size, we fitted a mixed logistic model of switching as a function of confidence with random intercepts and slopes (two of the models were the same as the ones described above).
We fitted similar models using accuracy (PC) instead of confidence to compare how they predict switching.

Finally, for each window size, we measured and tested the correlation between confidence and PC defined with the same window size (e.g., how does average confidence in the last n trials correlate with average accuracy in the last n trials?).

text.text: These results give us several clues that informed our modeling decisions.
(1) The correlations between confidence and PC are reliable, but rather weak, even for larger window sizes (peaking at about .27).
This suggests that subjective confidence tracks objective accuracy but is poorly calibrated due to unaccounted effects and measurement noise.
(2) PC measures defined over longer windows account for switching behavior better than measures defined over smaller window sizes.
(3) Measures of confidence seem to have a weaker effect on switching, compared to the more objective PC measures.
Crucially, confidence measures fail to account for switching when defined on larger window sizes, suggesting that, perhaps, these measures accumulate too much noise to reliably predict decisions.
Thus, confidence measures defined over smaller window sizes may explain switching above and beyond the most predictive measures of PC.
Given these results, we defined subjective task confidence as a running mean of trial-wise confidence judgments over the last 4 trials, which is the window size at which we saw the largest effect.

Repetition bias in self-directed learning
Conditional logit models quantify the extent to which each task feature is represented in participants' choices.
These models assume that each choice is an independent decision which makes them appropriate for describing how learners select tasks to engage with.
However, self-directed learning can be viewed as involving qualitatively different decisions: which task to engage with (selection) and when to disengage from the selected task (sustenance).
While the analyses above quantify the high degree of choice repetition, they tell us little of how it might be modulated by epistemic factors.
I.e. they do not explain how blocking is sustained over time.

To investigate whether repetition is modulated by epistemic predictors, we fitted a discrete time survival-analysis model (Singer & Willett, 1993) where the hazardous event is the last trial of a block.

text.text: We coded each trial of each block according to whether that trial was the last trial of the block and excluded trial 180 on which the event occurrence was ambiguous.

We then regressed this variable on a set of predictors, including the log of block trial, PC (and LP, and CONF) of the task in the current block, the average PC (and LP, and CONF) of the unchosen tasks, and the relative novelty of the current block's task: lastBlockTrial ∼ logBlockTrial + NOV current-others + PC current + LP current + CONF current + PC others + LP others + CONF others + (Rand | id), where Rand stands for participant random intercepts and slopes for each of the fixed predictors.
All predictors (except logBlockTrial) were centered around participants' means.
The negative and significant coefficients for the intercept and block trial confirm the tendency to block.

The random model is Y t ∼ Categorical([ 1 3 , 1 3 , 1 3 ]).

The probability that Y t = Y t+1 is p = k 1 3 × 13 = 39 = 1 3 .

In 179 pairs of adjacent trials, the expected number of switching is 179 × 23 ≈ 119.3.
A block is defined as sequence of non-switch trials.

Figure1: Task and stimuli.
A. The main task consisted of 180 trials with the same structure.
Each trial started with a self-paced choice screen, on which the participant was prompted to choose a family to interact with.

After making a choice, the participant was presented with a randomly drawn individual from the chosen family (see B) and was prompted to indicate what they thought this individual preferred to eat (as well as how confident they were in their guess).
The guess and the confidence level were measured using a single slider widget.
Moving the slider closer to one of the answer options indicated more confidence in that option.
Placing the slider thumb in the middle of the slider deactivated the submit button underneath, while placing it anywhere else activated it.
Thus, participants were forced to guess one of the options but could indicate their level of confidence.
As a visual aid, a confidence scale appeared underneath the option that the participant was committing to.
This scale reflected the confidence level (from one's subjective minimum to their subjective maximum) that corresponded to the position of the slider thumb.
Upon clicking the submit button, participants were given visual and auditory feedback signifying if the monster had accepted the food (saying "Yum") or rejected it (saying "Yuck").
B. Each family consisted of 30 unique individuals.
The example above shows all members of the "blue bears" family.
The individuals varied along 2 dimensions (e.g., height and width).
The classification rule was based on the combination of the two dimensions.
Individuals whose sum of values on both dimensions exceeded 7 preferred one type of food.
Individuals whose sum of values on both dimensions was less than 7 preferred the other type of food.
We excluded monsters whose sum of features was equal to 7 to keep the symmetry of the rule and keep food preferences in each family balanced.
